passage:
In the creche on the ground floor of a Mumbai housing society, Gargi, five, snatched the red tricycle from little Tuhin. He sat down hard and wailed.
Neelam aunty, who ran the creche, didn't scold. She crouched beside Gargi and took out a set of face cards. "Which face is Tuhin making?"
Gargi pointed to the crying one.
"And why might he feel like that?"
Gargi looked at the tricycle, then at Tuhin. "Because I took it." She rolled it back to him. "You go one round, then me."
Neelam aunty nodded. "When I have to wait, I feel happy if someone shares."

qa.q: What did Gargi snatch from Tuhin?
qa.a: The red tricycle.

qa.q: What did Gargi realise when she looked from the tricycle to Tuhin?
qa.a: Gargi realised Tuhin was upset because she had taken the tricycle, and she seemed sorry, seeing his feeling as separate from her own wish to ride.

qa.q: Why was asking about the face card a better choice than scolding?
qa.a: It let Gargi work out Tuhin's feeling herself, so she chose to share rather than just obeying an order.

qa.q: How might Tuhin see the moment Gargi rolls the tricycle back?
qa.a: Tuhin probably feels his upset has been noticed and put right, and he gets his turn after all.

grounding: A creche carer uses face cards, a question about another child's feeling, and her own example to help a five-year-old see the other side.

passage:
"Mine! Sam can't touch it!" Anjali hugged the block castle.
Elizabeth sat down on the rug with Teddy. "Oh dear. Teddy wanted to help build too." She made Teddy's head droop. "How does Teddy feel now?"
"Sad, Mama. His head's down."
"Hmm. Who else is looking at the castle with his head down?"
Anjali peeked at her little brother, Sam, who was sucking his thumb by the sofa. "Sam is."
"When I can't join in, I feel left out," said Elizabeth. "What could Sam do?"
"He can do the door part," Anjali said, and held out one block.

qa.q: Who was sucking his thumb by the sofa?
qa.a: Anjali's little brother, Sam.

qa.q: What does Anjali's 'Sam is' suggest she has started to think?
qa.a: Anjali has started to notice that Sam might feel like Teddy, left out and sad, when a moment ago only her castle mattered.

qa.q: Which of Elizabeth's choices helped Anjali share without being told to?
qa.a: Using Teddy for pretend play, then saying how she herself feels when left out, so Anjali could spot Sam's feeling on her own.

qa.q: If you were Sam, what would that one block mean to you?
qa.a: It would mean finally being let in after watching from the sofa, and getting to build the door 🙂

grounding: A mother uses pretend play with a teddy and her own feelings to help her daughter see her little brother's point of view.

passage:
Class note, Tuesday: Simran (5)
During story time Simran laughed when Dev's paper boat tore, and Dev crawled under the table. I didn't ask Simran to say sorry straight away. I opened the picture book to the page where the bear's kite breaks and asked, "What is the bear feeling?"
"Sad. He liked it."
Then I said, "I think Dev liked his boat too."
Simran went quiet, then went and fetched the tape.
Next step: puppet play on Thursday about taking turns and saying sorry. 🙂
— Maria

qa.q: Whose paper boat tore during story time?
qa.a: Dev's paper boat.

qa.q: Why did Simran go quiet after Maria's words about Dev?
qa.a: Simran seemed to link the sad bear with Dev and realise the boat had mattered to Dev, something the laughing had missed.

qa.q: Why did Maria choose the picture book over an instant 'say sorry'?
qa.a: The picture let Simran find the feeling first, so fetching the tape came from understanding rather than an order.

qa.q: What was the torn boat like for Dev?
qa.a: Dev lost something he liked and was laughed at as well, so crawling under the table was a way to get away from both.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a picture book and a gentle comparison helping a five-year-old imagine a classmate's feeling.

passage: At the anganwadi in a village near Sagar, Siddharth, five, snatched the only toy tractor from Pradeep, whose face crumpled into a howl. Sunita didi, the anganwadi worker, didn't scold. She knelt and held up a picture card of a crying child. "Look at this face. What happened, do you think?" "Someone took the thing," Siddharth said. "And how is Pradeep's face now?" Siddharth looked. "Same." Sunita didi picked up two cloth dolls. "Let's play. This doll had the tractor. What does it say?" Siddharth made the doll say, "Give back!" Then he slowly held out the tractor.

qa.q: What did Sunita didi hold up after Siddharth snatched the tractor?
qa.a: A picture card of a crying child.

qa.q: What did Siddharth seem to realise when he said Pradeep's face was "Same"?
qa.a: He was beginning to see that Pradeep felt like the child in the picture, upset because something was taken.

qa.q: Why did the doll game work better than a scolding?
qa.a: Speaking for the doll let Siddharth feel what Pradeep felt, so he chose to give the tractor back himself.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when Siddharth held out the tractor?
qa.a: Pradeep would likely feel relieved and cared for, seeing that the other child noticed the hurt.

grounding: A caregiver uses a picture card and pretend play to help a child see how another child feels.

passage: At a playgroup in Cape Town, Lucia, four, laughed when Thabo's sandcastle collapsed. Thabo's lip wobbled. Their teacher, Mrs Dlamini, sat down in the sand. "Lucia, when my tower falls down, I feel sad inside. How do you think Thabo feels?" Lucia shrugged. "It's funny." Mrs Dlamini held up a small plastic figure. "This is Thabo. His castle just fell. Can you make him talk?" Lucia took it and said in a tiny voice, "My castle is broken." She stopped smiling. "Thabo, want help?" she asked, and began patting the sand.

qa.q: What happened to Thabo's sandcastle?
qa.a: It collapsed.

qa.q: What changed in Lucia's mind while she made the figure talk?
qa.a: Speaking as Thabo let her feel his sadness, so the fall stopped seeming funny and she wanted to help.

qa.q: Which of Mrs Dlamini's moves helped most, and why?
qa.a: Sharing her own feeling first and then using the figure for pretend play, which showed Lucia how to imagine Thabo's side.

qa.q: How might Thabo feel when Lucia offers to help?
qa.a: Thabo would likely feel comforted, since the child who laughed now sees his disappointment and wants to rebuild with him.

grounding: A teacher models naming her own feelings and uses pretend play to help a young child take another child's view.

passage: In the Kochi preschool, Aadhya pulled the doll out of Ishita's arms. Ishita burst into tears. The teacher sat down with both girls and a set of face cards. "Aadhya, which face is Ishita making?" Aadhya pointed at the crying face. "Why do you think she feels like that?" "She wanted the doll." "Mm. How would you feel if someone took your doll?" Aadhya looked at the angry card. "Cross." The teacher nodded. "Ishita feels sad and cross. What could help?" Aadhya held the doll out. Ishita sniffed and took it.

qa.q: What did the teacher use to talk with the girls?
qa.a: A set of face cards.

qa.q: What did the teacher want Aadhya to understand by asking how she would feel?
qa.a: The teacher hoped Aadhya would feel what Ishita felt, sad and cross, by imagining it happening to herself.

qa.q: Why do face cards work well for children this age?
qa.a: Pictures give young children a simple way to see and name another child's feelings before they can explain them in words.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Aadhya holds the doll out?
qa.a: Ishita probably feels relieved and a bit comforted, seeing Aadhya understand she was upset.

grounding: Shows a caregiver using pictures and questions about another child's feelings to help a preschooler take another's viewpoint.

passage: From our balcony in Bhopal I can see straight into the neighbours' front room. Last evening, five-year-old Wasim knocked down his baby sister's block tower and laughed. She wailed. His uncle, Pankaj, didn't shout. He fetched two sock puppets. One puppet built a tower; the other knocked it over. "Oh no," said the first puppet, in a small voice. "I worked so hard on that." Pankaj asked Wasim, "What is this puppet feeling?" Wasim was quiet for a moment, watching. "Sad." Then he picked up the blocks and started building again for his sister. I couldn't hear everything after that. But I saw him hand her the top block.

qa.q: What did Pankaj fetch after the tower fell?
qa.a: Two sock puppets.

qa.q: What did Pankaj seem to hope for when he asked what the puppet was feeling?
qa.a: Pankaj seemed calm and patient, hoping Wasim would notice his sister's sadness through the puppet rather than through a scolding.

qa.q: Why might pretend play work better than shouting here?
qa.a: Seeing it happen to a puppet lets Wasim step outside himself and feel how the tower-builder feels, without being defensive.

qa.q: How might Wasim's sister feel when he hands her the top block?
qa.a: She likely feels comforted and included, and her upset eases as her tower is rebuilt.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's account, a caregiver using pretend play to help a young child see how another feels.

passage:
Monday: At the park, Aditi's friend tripped and scraped her knee. Aditi laughed. Reena, her mother, knelt down. "Look at her face. How do you think her knee feels?" Aditi stopped laughing. "Ouchy."
Wednesday: At home, Reena and Aditi played doctor with a teddy. Reena said, "Teddy fell. I think Teddy feels sore and scared. What can we say?" Aditi patted the teddy. "Are you okay?"
Saturday: A boy on the slide bumped his head. Aditi ran up to him first. "Does it hurt?"

qa.q: What did Aditi's friend scrape at the park?
qa.a: Her knee.

qa.q: Why did Reena ask Aditi to look at her friend's face?
qa.a: Reena felt concerned that Aditi had laughed, and wanted to help her notice the friend's pain by reading her face.

qa.q: What helped Aditi most between Monday and Saturday?
qa.a: Pretend play with the teddy, where Reena modelled saying how someone else feels, gave Aditi practice she then used at the slide.

qa.q: How might the boy on the slide feel when Aditi runs up to him?
qa.a: He probably feels cared for and less alone after bumping his head.

grounding: Shows a caregiver asking what another child feels and modelling it in pretend play, so a preschooler's empathy grows over days.

passage:
The daycare had only ten minutes before pickup, and the room was noisy. Tanvir, five, grabbed a toy truck from another boy, who started to cry.

The caregiver, Himani, knelt beside Tanvir. "Look at his face. How do you think he feels?"

Tanvir looked. "Sad."

"How do you feel when someone takes your truck?"

"Sad. And angry."

Himani held up a picture card of a crying face. "Like this?"

Tanvir nodded, then handed the truck back. "Sorry."

Himani smiled. "Maybe you can play together?"

The two boys pushed the truck back and forth until the parents came.

qa.q: What did Himani hold up?
qa.a: A picture card of a crying face.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel after Himani's questions?
qa.a: He felt a little sorry and understanding, recognising the other boy felt sad like he would.

qa.q: What did Himani do to help Tanvir see the other boy's view?
qa.a: She asked him to look at the boy's face, linked it to his own feelings and used a picture card, even with little time.

qa.q: How might the other boy feel when Tanvir says sorry?
qa.a: The other boy probably feels comforted and happy to play again.

grounding: Under time pressure, a caregiver helps a preschooler think about another child's feelings using questions and a picture card.

passage:
During Pongal, the Chennai playschool set up a pretend kitchen. Vasudha, four, wanted to cook alone and pushed Divyansh away.

Her teacher knelt down with two dolls. "This doll wants to cook too. How do you think she feels?"

"Sad," said Vasudha.

"And if someone pushed you away from the pot?"

"I'd cry."

"So what could we do?"

Vasudha thought. "He can stir. I can put the rice."

Divyansh stirred proudly. The teacher said, "See? Now Divyansh feels happy too." Vasudha beamed.

qa.q: What did the playschool set up during Pongal?
qa.a: A pretend kitchen.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when she pictured being pushed away herself?
qa.a: She felt she would be sad enough to cry, which helped her understand Divyansh.

qa.q: How did the teacher use pretend play to help Vasudha?
qa.a: The teacher used dolls to show another's feelings, then asked how Vasudha would feel, helping her think of sharing.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel after Vasudha let him stir?
qa.a: Divyansh felt happy and proud.

grounding: A caregiver uses dolls and pretend play to help a preschooler take another child's view.

passage:
"Baljeet, Pankaj is crying. What happened?"

"He knocked my tower."

"Did he mean to?"

"I don't know."

"Let's ask him. Pankaj, did you mean to?"

Pankaj shook his head. "My foot slipped."

"Oh. How do you think Pankaj feels now?"

Baljeet looked. "Sad. Because I shouted."

"When I see a friend crying, I say, 'Are you okay?' Want to try?"

Baljeet mumbled, "Are you okay?"

Pankaj nodded. The rain outside kept falling, and they built a new tower together.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj knock the tower?
qa.a: His foot slipped.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when he saw Pankaj crying?
qa.a: Baljeet felt a bit sorry, realising Pankaj was sad because of the shouting.

qa.q: What did the adult model to help Baljeet?
qa.a: The adult showed how to ask a friend "Are you okay?", modelling how to notice others' feelings.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel when Baljeet asks if he's okay?
qa.a: Pankaj probably feels comforted and relieved.

grounding: A caregiver asks how another child feels and models caring words, helping a preschooler grow in empathy.

passage: Class note, Christmas week. Rashmi grabbed the angel costume from Ritu and ran. Ritu cried. I asked Rashmi, "Look at Ritu's face. What do you think she's feeling?" Rashmi said, "Happy?" We looked at our feelings chart together, and she pointed to "sad". Then we played a quick pretend game with two dolls, one taking a toy from the other. Rashmi made the doll say, "That's mine, I'm sad!" She went and gave the costume back. Tomorrow we will act out sharing again.

qa.q: What did Rashmi grab from Ritu?
qa.a: The angel costume.

qa.q: What did Rashmi first think Ritu was feeling, and why?
qa.a: Rashmi guessed "happy", because she herself was happy with the costume and couldn't yet see Ritu's side; the chart helped her see the sadness.

qa.q: Which tools did the teacher use?
qa.a: Asking about Ritu's face, a feelings chart, and pretend play with dolls, so Rashmi could see the other side.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel when the costume comes back?
qa.a: Relieved and comforted, though perhaps still a little wary.

grounding: A caregiver uses questions, a feelings chart and pretend play to help a preschooler see another child's feelings.

passage: On Lohri evening in the village, Himani wouldn't let her younger cousin Tushar near the bonfire popcorn. "Mine!" Dadi sat both children on her charpai. "Himani, if Tushar had all the popcorn, how would your tummy feel?" Himani thought. "Empty. Angry." "And how is Tushar's tummy now?" Himani peeked at him; his lip was wobbling. Dadi picked up two small clay cups. "Let's pretend this cup is Himani and this one is Tushar. What does Tushar-cup say?" Himani made the cup squeak, "I want some too!" Then she tipped popcorn into his hands.

qa.q: What wouldn't Himani let Tushar near?
qa.a: The bonfire popcorn.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when she imagined Tushar having all the popcorn?
qa.a: She said her tummy would feel empty and angry, which helped her connect to how Tushar felt.

qa.q: How did Dadi build Himani's perspective taking?
qa.a: She asked how Himani would feel in Tushar's place and used two clay cups for pretend play, so Himani voiced Tushar's view.

qa.q: What might Tushar feel when Himani shares?
qa.a: He is likely happy and relieved after feeling left out.

grounding: A grandmother uses questions and pretend play with cups to help a preschooler take another child's view.

passage: On Three Kings morning in Seville, Alejandro tore open his new train and wouldn't let his little brother Pablo touch it. Pablo sobbed. Papá knelt down with the picture book they had been reading. "Look, here's the bear who wouldn't share. How does the little bear feel?" Alejandro pointed. "Sad. Crying." "Who does he look like?" Alejandro looked at Pablo. "Pablo." Papá said gently, "From where Pablo sits, the train is shiny and far away." Alejandro pushed one carriage over. "This one's yours."

qa.q: What did Alejandro get on Three Kings morning?
qa.a: A new train.

qa.q: What did Alejandro feel when he saw that the sad bear looked like Pablo?
qa.a: He seemed to feel a pang of sympathy, linking the bear's sadness to his brother's.

qa.q: How did Papá help Alejandro see Pablo's side?
qa.a: He used a picture book, asked how the little bear felt, and said aloud how things looked from where Pablo sat.

qa.q: How might Pablo feel when he gets a carriage?
qa.a: He is probably comforted and happy to be included.

grounding: A parent uses a picture book and modelled words to help a preschooler see his brother's view.

passage: It was kite week before Sankranti at the community centre crèche, and paper diamonds hung from every window. Ganga yanked the pink kite out of little Rashi's hands. Rashi howled. Farida, the teacher, knelt beside Ganga with her box of face cards. "Which face is Rashi making?" Ganga pointed at the crying card. "Sad." "Why sad?" Ganga thought. "Kite gone." Farida said, "From where Rashi stands, the kite just disappeared." She picked up two sock puppets. "This one is Ganga, this one is Rashi. Show me." Ganga made her puppet grab, then stopped. "Rashi puppet cries," she said quietly, and carried the real kite back.

qa.q: What did Farida use to help Ganga?
qa.a: She used a box of face cards and two sock puppets.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she made her puppet stop grabbing?
qa.a: She seemed sorry and a little ashamed, because acting out the grab let her feel what losing the kite was like for Rashi.

qa.q: Which choice by Farida worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Ganga to name Rashi's face and replay it with puppets worked, because Ganga found the other child's feeling herself instead of just being scolded.

qa.q: How might Rashi see the moment Ganga brings the kite back?
qa.a: Rashi would likely feel relieved and surprised, and may trust Ganga more when they play together next time.

grounding: A caregiver uses picture cards, pretend play and her own words about another child's view to help a preschooler take that child's perspective.
